title: Badinerie in Close-Up: Binary Form, Virtuosity and Baroque Devices
content_html:
Recap: Binary Form and Why Badinerie Is a Perfect Case Study

Badinerie is the final movement of Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, BWV 1067, scored for solo flute, strings and continuo. Its French title means ‘joke’ or ‘banter’, and the music lives up to the name: a fast 2/4 dance full of energy, wit and dazzling flute writing. Because the movement is built entirely from binary form, it is one of the clearest possible examples for your listening exam of how this structure actually works in a real piece.

Binary form has two sections, A and B, both usually repeated, giving the pattern AABB. This is different from ternary form (ABA), where the opening material returns at the end. In Badinerie there is no literal restatement of the A section within B — instead, B takes the music further away harmonically before steering it back home for the final cadence. Understanding exactly what happens harmonically in each half is the key skill examiners test.

The A Section: B Minor to D Major

The A section opens firmly in the tonic key, B minor, with the flute launching straight into its rapid semiquaver theme over a supportive string and continuo accompaniment. As the section progresses, the harmony moves away from B minor towards a new key, arriving at a perfect cadence that confirms F sharp minor by the end of the section. This modulation to the relative major is the textbook harmonic plan for a minor-key binary movement, and it is exactly what you should listen for and be ready to name.

Exam-ready fact: the relative major of a minor key is built on the third degree of that minor scale. B minor and D major share the same key signature (two sharps), which is why this modulation sounds so smooth — it is a shift of colour rather than a jolt.

The B Section: Further Modulation and the Return to B Minor

The B section begins in the F sharp minor established at the close of A, but Bach does not let the music rest there. It travels through further related keys — including a passage that touches on F sharp minor, the dominant minor of B minor — before the harmony is steered firmly back to the home key of B minor for the movement’s final cadence. This constant harmonic movement, always circling back towards the tonic, is what gives binary form its sense of a satisfying journey rather than a static repeat.

One device that drives this harmonic movement is sequence: a short melodic or rhythmic idea is repeated immediately at a different pitch level, usually stepping up or down. Sequences appear throughout Badinerie’s semiquaver passages and are a favourite exam target, because spotting one and naming it correctly earns easy identification marks.

Virtuosic Flute Writing and Semiquaver Figuration

The flute part in Badinerie is famously virtuosic. Almost the entire melodic line is built from continuous semiquaver figuration — fast scalic runs and broken-chord (arpeggio) patterns that demand rapid, even fingerwork from the soloist. Performers also need strong breath control, since phrases run on for many bars without an obvious place to breathe, and clear articulation, often using double-tonguing, to keep every note crisp at such a fast tempo.

Underneath this virtuoso display, the strings mostly play sustained chords or simple quaver-based patterns. This creates a melody-dominated homophonic texture: one virtuosic line supported by a much simpler accompaniment, so the flute is never in competition for the listener’s attention.

Terraced Dynamics and the Continuo Role

Baroque instruments, especially the harpsichord, could not produce a smooth, gradual crescendo or diminuendo the way a modern piano can. Composers of this period instead used terraced dynamics: sudden shifts between loud and soft, often created by repeating a phrase quietly straight after it has been heard loudly, producing an echo effect. Listen for these abrupt dynamic blocks rather than any gradual dynamic shading in Badinerie.

Exam wording tip: describe this feature as ‘terraced dynamics’, not just ‘the volume changes suddenly’. Naming the correct technical term, rather than describing the effect in vague words, is what separates a top-band answer from a middle-band one.

Answering Forms-and-Devices Questions on Badinerie

Questions on this piece may ask you to identify the structure, name the key relationship between sections, spot a cadence, or describe the dynamics, texture or continuo role at a given point. Because Badinerie is short and highly repetitive in its figuration, examiners often use it to test whether you can pinpoint exactly where a modulation or dynamic change happens.

Always use precise musical vocabulary: binary form, relative major, terraced dynamics, continuo, sequence, semiquaver figuration. A vague answer such as ‘it changes key and gets louder’ will score fewer marks than one that names the specific device and, where relevant, the specific keys involved.

Model phrasing for a strong answer: ‘The A section modulates from the tonic, B minor, to F sharp minor, the dominant minor, confirmed by a perfect cadence, while terraced dynamics create an echo effect between the string and flute phrases.’ This single sentence covers structure, key relationship, cadence and dynamics in one precise statement.
exam_tip_html: When a question gives you a bar number or timing and asks what happens there, do not just describe the mood — name the device and its function: for example, instead of writing 'the flute plays fast notes here', write 'continuous semiquaver figuration built from a rising sequence, supported by sustained string chords', since examiners reward technical precision over general impressions; a common mistake is confusing 'relative major' with 'tonic major', so always check whether the new key shares the same key signature (relative) or the same keynote (tonic major/minor) before naming it.
conclusion_html: Badinerie packs binary form, modulation, sequence, terraced dynamics and virtuosic writing into just a few minutes of music, making it one of the richest pieces for forms-and-devices practice — now test yourself by re-listening and pinpointing each device at the exact moment it occurs.

practice_questions.text: Name the overall structure of Badinerie.
practice_questions.marks: Award the mark for 'binary form' (accept AABB).

practice_questions.text: State the tonic key and the key reached by the end of the A section.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for B minor (tonic), one mark for F sharp minor (dominant minor, reached by the end of A).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the modulation from B minor to F sharp minor sounds smooth rather than abrupt.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for reference to the two keys being relative major/minor and sharing the same key signature (two sharps).

practice_questions.text: Describe the dynamic technique used in Badinerie and explain why Baroque composers relied on it.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for naming terraced dynamics, describing sudden loud/soft contrast or echo effect, and linking this to the limitations of Baroque instruments such as the harpsichord.

practice_questions.text: Identify two features of the flute writing that make it virtuosic.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark each for any two of: continuous semiquaver runs, scalic/arpeggio patterns, wide leaps, need for breath control, need for fast articulation/double-tonguing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the continuo in Badinerie and how it differs from the flute's role.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for identifying harpsichord and cello/bass as continuo, describing their harmonic/rhythmic supporting function, and contrasting this with the flute's virtuosic melodic role, creating a melody-dominated homophonic texture.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the tonic key of Badinerie?
What key does the A section modulate to by its close?
Which term describes a short musical idea repeated immediately at a different pitch?
Which best describes the dynamics typically used in Badinerie?
options: Terraced dynamics with sudden loud/soft contrasts

knowledge_checks.q: Which instruments typically make up the continuo in this piece?

glossary_terms.definition: A two-part musical structure, A and B, usually each repeated, common in Baroque dance movements.
The major key built on the third degree of a minor scale, sharing the same key signature as that minor key.
The minor key built on the fifth degree of a scale, a related key often visited during modulation.
The process of changing from one key to another within a piece of music.
Sudden shifts between loud and soft dynamic levels, without gradual crescendo or diminuendo, typical of Baroque music.
A Baroque accompanying group, typically harpsichord and a bass instrument such as cello, providing harmonic and rhythmic foundation.
Fast melodic patterns made up of semiquavers, often scalic or arpeggio-based, requiring virtuosic technique.
Describing music or a performance that demands exceptional technical skill from the performer.
A short melodic or rhythmic idea repeated immediately at a different pitch level.
A pair of chords ending a musical phrase, giving a sense of pause or conclusion.
